notes: Previous finding S1 (A2: no NSGs) is RESOLVED at c4032df. network.bicep declares two NSGs and attaches both to their subnets. The private-endpoint subnet sets privateEndpointNetworkPolicies 'Enabled', so the NSG applies to the endpoint's traffic. The rule is allow-sql-from-app-and-agents at priority 100: Tcp, source [appIntegrationPrefix, agentAddressPrefix], destination the endpoint subnet, port 1433 only. It is followed by deny-all-inbound at 4000, which overrides the default AllowVnetInBound at 65000. The app-integration subnet has deny-all-inbound only, which is correct because App Service VNet integration is outbound-only and no inbound path is needed.

NSG rules judged for what they introduce: no new weakness found. (1) The deny sits at 4000, well below the allow, so rule order is correct. (2) Only 1433 is allowed. A private endpoint to Azure SQL uses the Proxy connection mode on 1433, so no 11000-11999 range is needed, and none is opened. (3) The source prefixes are specific CIDRs, not '*' or a service tag. (4) Outbound is left at the defaults. The app's outbound goes to SQL and App Insights, and an outbound allow-list on the integration subnet would be extra hardening, not a defect. (5) Peered agent traffic keeps its source IP, so agentAddressPrefix matches it. (6) The committed placeholder 10.30.0.0/24 does not overlap 10.20.0.0/16 and fails closed: an unset value blocks the agents, it does not open SQL. The param-file comments say to set it before the first deployment.

Hygiene observation, not a finding: agentAddressPrefix is a bare string with no validation. An operator who set it to '0.0.0.0/0' or '10.0.0.0/8' would widen the 1433 allow rule. SQL stays Entra-only with public access disabled, and the value comes from a reviewed param file, so the risk is low. A @minLength or a documented expectation of a narrow /24-ish range would be a reasonable README line. It is not worth a code change.

R2 change (SQL service connection as a compile-time template parameter): sc-policies-<env>-sql are connection names, not credentials. The two SQL steps still use ${{ parameters.sqlServiceConnection }} and not the ARM connection, so the least-privilege split from A2 is intact. The Deploy app and infrastructure steps use the ARM connection only. The pool is policies-<env>-vnet.

R4 comment rewording is accurate: it states that the ARM connection holds subscription-scope rights, so a leaked ARM token could rewrite the SQL Entra admin through ARM, that this is accepted residual risk, and that the first run fails until the one-off bootstrap has been run. It overstates nothing, and it tells the reader where the trust boundary sits.

Unchanged since A2 and re-checked: SQL publicNetworkAccess Disabled, no 0.0.0.0 rule, Entra-only authentication with no password, a private endpoint with a privatelink DNS zone, basic-auth publishing disabled for scm and ftp, dotnet-ef pinned to 10.0.13 (equals the EF Core Design version), tenant from tenant(). The -Q string interpolates only $(appName) and a hex SID, both derived from deployment outputs, so it is not attacker-controlled. No secrets, local paths or personal emails in infrastructure/. The param files hold all-zero placeholder GUIDs.

Out-of-scope items recorded as n/a. API1:2023: no auth or tenancy. API2:2023: auth is out of scope; the infrastructure identity design is sound as reviewed in A2. API5:2023: no roles. API7:2023: no outbound URL fetching, and the diff touches no src/. API10:2023: no upstream APIs.
